title: Block close: the great conversation
hook: two thousand years of thinkers arguing, praying and adding

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Polkinghorne and the kettle: how it boils, and why. Your line was two windows.

A long table, and the chairs keep filling. At one end, Justin, a teacher in Rome, says the seeds of the Word were scattered everywhere, even among the philosophers. Further down, Augustine confesses to God out loud. Boethius talks with Philosophy in his cell. Anselm tries to think the greatest thing that can be thought. Julian of Norwich, quietly: all shall be well. Luther bangs the table about grace. Pascal mutters about reasons of the heart. Kierkegaard insists on the single person. Bonhoeffer writes questions from prison. At the near end, the newest arrivals: a priest-physicist, a teacher from the rice fields, a scholar from Kenya. Nobody here agrees about everything. Today the block of great thinkers closes with a step back to see the whole table.
screen: `STEP BACK AND SEE THE WHOLE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Some call it the great conversation, centuries long. Four things stand out. First, they argued. Anselm built an argument; others pushed back. Aquinas set out his five ways; Ockham shaved away what he thought wasn't needed. Luther and the Catholic thinkers who answered him disagreed deeply. Second, they prayed. Augustine wrote his Confessions as a long prayer. Dionysius climbed a ladder of names into silence. Simone Weil said attention, at its highest, is prayer. For several of them, thinking about God and talking to God were one act. Third, they added. Nobody started from zero. Newman said doctrine grows, like a seed into a tree. Ware handed on the Orthodox way. Mbiti and Koyama asked what the gospel sounds like in their own soil. The letter to the Hebrews pictures the faithful of the past as a crowd in the stands: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight." Fourth, they never finished. The preacher in Ecclesiastes warned, a little wearily: "of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh." The books kept coming anyway, and so did the conversation. That's the good news of an unfinished table: there's still a chair. Anyone who reads, asks, doubts, prays, or writes in a margin is already taking part.

Let the faces of this block pass by, Augustine, Boethius, Julian, Aquinas, Luther, Pascal, Wesley, Kierkegaard, Bonhoeffer, Weil, Merton, Ware, Koyama, Mbiti, Polkinghorne and the rest, and notice the one whose question is also yours, not the one you think you should choose. Let that one take a seat beside you. If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, just hold their question for a moment.
Block close. The end of the great thinkers: people who argued, prayed and added, around a table that still has room.
Your line: join the conversation. Centuries of voices, and room for one more. And that closes the block.

howItsDone: Christians read the great thinkers of their tradition in study groups, seminaries and on their own, often keeping a favorite writer for years.

chat.says: You've been reading old Christian thinkers for weeks. Did they all end up agreeing?
options: No. They argued, prayed and built on each other, and the conversation still isn't finished.
Yes. By the end they had settled every big question, so there's nothing left to add.
No. They mostly worked alone, and none of them read or answered the others.
chat.meaning: The great thinkers argued, prayed and added to what came before, and the conversation never finished, so there's still a chair for anyone.

Justin.meaning: an early Christian teacher in Rome

Boethius.meaning: a Roman thinker who wrote of talking with Philosophy in his cell

Julian of Norwich.meaning: English writer remembered for the words: all shall be well

Ockham.meaning: a thinker who shaved away what he thought wasn't needed

Kierkegaard.meaning: a thinker who insisted on the single person
